questions.q: After the seventh Venus flyby, how long does Parker take to go once around the Sun, and what is its published top speed?
questions.do: Drag the After Venus flyby slider to 7 and read Lap time and Top speed, published in the This orbit box.
questions.a: 88 days and 192 km/s. Each flyby shrank the orbit, so the lap got shorter and the top speed got higher.

questions.q: Which needs a bigger push from Earth's orbit: leaving the solar system for ever, or hitting the Sun's surface?
questions.do: Look at the bar chart in Why the Sun is so hard to reach. Compare the bars Leave the solar system for ever and Hit the Sun's surface.
questions.a: Hitting the Sun needs about 26.9 km/s, more than twice the 12.3 km/s needed to leave the solar system. To fall into the Sun you must cancel almost all of Earth's 29.8 km/s sideways speed.

questions.q: How much stronger is sunlight at closest approach after flyby 1 compared with after flyby 7?
questions.do: Set the After Venus flyby slider to 1 and read the sunlight line under This orbit. Then move it to 7 and read it again.
questions.a: About 36 times Earth's sunlight after flyby 1, and about 476 times after flyby 7 (NASA quotes 475). Sunlight grows as one over distance squared, and the closest distance fell from 24.81 to 6.86 million km.

questions.q: Parker's rocket gave it only about 12.7 km/s. Why could it not fly straight to its final orbit at 9.86 solar radii?
questions.do: In the bar chart, compare What Parker's rocket gave it, worked out from its first orbit with Reach Parker's final 9.86 solar radii, directly. Then press Play the seven years to watch the orbit shrink.
questions.a: Going there directly needs about 21.0 km/s, but the rocket gave only 12.7 km/s. So Parker used seven Venus passes, each one shedding a little more speed, to shrink the orbit step by step.

questions.q: The header says that on 24 December 2024 Parker passed 6.16 million km above the Sun's surface. The lab shows a different closest distance. Why do the two numbers differ?
questions.do: Set the After Venus flyby slider to 7 and read Closest to the Sun's centre. Compare it with the header text and the solar radius in the footer.
questions.a: The lab shows 6.86 million km from the Sun's centre. Subtract the solar radius, 695,700 km (about 0.70 million km), and you get about 6.16 million km above the surface. That 2024 pass, at 191 km/s, is the fastest anything people have built has gone.
